subsystems.name: Plume-traversal and grain capture
subsystems.role: fly the spacecraft through the plume fast enough to reach it but survive the encounter.
parts: optical and dust detectors to sense the plume

subsystems.name: Inlet and ionisation
subsystems.role: take in ice grains travelling at kilometres per second and turn them into ions.

subsystems.name: Mass analyser
subsystems.role: weighs ions and their fragments to identify molecules.

subsystems.name: Chiral separation stage
subsystems.role: tells left-handed from right-handed molecules — a strong biosignature.

subsystems.name: Cleanliness and blanking system
subsystems.role: stops the spacecraft's own organic material looking like life.

subsystems.name: Ground interpretation
subsystems.role: turns spectra into a defensible claim about biology.

buildSteps.title: Define the biosignatures
buildSteps.detail: Pick molecules that abiotic chemistry struggles to make — amino acids, lipids, and a preference for one chirality over the other — and set a detection threshold before launch.

buildSteps.title: Build the mass spectrometer
buildSteps.detail: Compact an instrument that fills a lab bench into a box that survives launch, vacuum and radiation, using miniaturised time-of-flight or ion-trap components.

buildSteps.title: Build the separation stage
buildSteps.detail: Implement capillary electrophoresis — a thin tube where charged molecules migrate at different speeds — to separate structural and mirror-image variants before they reach the detector.

buildSteps.title: Test against analogue ice
buildSteps.detail: In a vacuum chamber, fire simulated plume grains at the inlet at hypervelocity and check that the instrument still recognises the molecules it was designed for.

buildSteps.title: Control contamination
buildSteps.detail: Assemble the sample path to organic-cleanliness standards, bake it out, and fly blanks so any signal can be compared against the spacecraft's own residues.

buildSteps.title: Integrate and shield
buildSteps.detail: Mount the instrument behind a dust shield with a clear view of the plume, and connect it to power, data and thermal control.

buildSteps.title: Fly the plume
buildSteps.detail: During a close pass, the inlet swallows grains; ions are separated, detected and the spectra stored.

buildSteps.title: Analyse on the ground
buildSteps.detail: Months later, the team compares returned spectra with libraries and reports a detection — or a limit.

prerequisites.why: a mass spectrometer on the Cassini mission proved grains can be ionised by impact and analysed during a flyby.
flight instruments can now resolve molecular masses closely enough to distinguish candidate biomolecules.
capillary electrophoresis has been demonstrated in laboratory and prototype form but not yet flown to an icy moon.
Enceladus plumes are sampled; a plume at Europa is suspected but unconfirmed.
organic contamination at parts-per-billion levels can mask or fake a detection.

pathway.milestone: mass spectrometers in cruise aboard Europa Clipper (launched 2024) and JUICE (launched 2023)
pathway.unlocks: the first detailed chemical survey of Europa's surface and environment.

pathway.milestone: dedicated multi-flyby plume-sampling missions to Enceladus with a full life-detection instrument suite
pathway.unlocks: repeated measurements that can be compared and replicated.

pathway.milestone: cryogenic sample return of plume ice to Earth laboratories
pathway.unlocks: analysis with instruments far more capable than anything that can be flown.

pathway.milestone: an orbiter or lander with an integrated suite at an ocean world
pathway.unlocks: a sustained search for life, and a way to confirm or refute a biosignature.
